  • GPT‑6 in ChatGPT introduces Intelligent UI, a latest capability that allows ChatGPT to answer quickly with fully interactive user interfaces that make everyday answers more visual, make learning complex topics easier and that can quickly create a tool to solve a task right in the moment.
  • According to recent reports, A 7‑speed bicycle brings together a frame, handlebars, wheels and hand-operated brakes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last month we introduced the first GPT‑6 models for paid customers and today we're bringing that next generation of intelligence to more people with a newly introduced GPT‑6 model built for more than 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT each week.

GPT‑6 in ChatGPT introduces Intelligent UI, a latest capability that allows ChatGPT to answer quickly with fully interactive user interfaces that make everyday answers more visual, make learning complex topics easier and that can quickly create a tool to solve a task right in the moment.

break down the design of a 7‑speed bike.

According to recent reports, A 7‑speed bicycle brings together a frame, handlebars, wheels and hand-operated brakes. Seven gears let the rider adjust pedaling effort as the drivetrain turns effort into motion.

Upright bars guide the steering, gears vary the effort, and hand brakes control the pace.

The frame carries the rider; the drivetrain turns effort into motion. Select a system to explore its role.

Industry observers note that two triangles connect the saddle, steering and pedals. The fork holds the front wheel and turns with the bars.

Spokes connect each hub to its rim and support the rider. The tires surround the rims and grip the ground.

Industry observers note that the pedals turn the chain, driving the rear wheel. Seven gears let the rider adjust pedaling effort for climbs, flats and descents.

Hand levers pull cables that bring the brake pads against the rims, turning a squeeze into controlled slowing.

Sources indicate that the handlebars and stem steer the front wheel. The saddle and seatpost support the rider and set the sitting position.

break down the design of a 7‑speed bike.

Sources indicate that A 7‑speed bicycle brings together a frame, handlebars, wheels and hand-operated brakes. Seven gears let the rider adjust pedaling effort as the drivetrain turns effort into motion.

Sources indicate that we’ve trained GPT‑6 to compose responses using text, visuals and interactive elements, choosing how they fit together based on your question. With Intelligent UI, responses can include graphics, tappable buttons, forms, charts, and interactive experiences you can use directly in your conversation.

The format depends on what you’re asking. A comparison might work best side by side. An explanation might be easier to understand through an interactive diagram. And when a simple text answer is the most useful response, ChatGPT can give you that.

In a recent development, chatGPT can make a proposal easier to follow by showing how it fits together. The timing for a Sunday roast can sit alongside the recipe, or the stops on a road trip can appear on a map, with notes on what’s worth a detour.

Visual and interactive explanations let you explore how something works, change an input to see what happens, or work through a problem step by step.

You can also ask ChatGPT to create a tool for the task at hand, such as a calculator to explore how savings could grow, a bill splitter for dinner with friends, or a game you can play in the conversation.

With Intelligent UI, we gave GPT‑6 the freedom to create the most useful interface for each question, while keeping the experience fast and familiar across web and mobile.

Recent findings suggest that we built a library of native, streamable components, along with a compiler that processes the interface as the model generates it. The library gives each response a familiar design foundation while leaving the model room to decide how the pieces fit together. The compiler allows the interface to appear progressively as the model generates it, without waiting for the entire response to be complete.

According to recent reports, we expanded our training methods to help the model make thoughtful decisions about content, layout, visuals, and interaction. This included evaluating the interfaces it creates for clarity, usefulness, and completeness. GPT‑6 learned to use the component library and make good design decisions, including how to organize information clearly, when to use interactivity, and when a simple text response is enough.

It has been revealed that there's still work ahead to improve the model's design judgment and expand what it can create, but Intelligent UI marks a significant shift in how people interact with ChatGPT. Instead of fitting every question into the same conversational format, ChatGPT can combine UI, data, and actions to create entirely fresh ways for people to explore, understand, and interact with information.

With GPT‑6, we’re also making it possible for ChatGPT to begin answering while it continues to think.

It has been revealed that with the introduction of reasoning models, owners could get help with much harder problems, but had to wait for the model to finish thinking before getting an answer. Now, ChatGPT can interleave thinking with answering. We trained it to take into account the user’s waiting time and progressively compose an answer using its knowledge and findings up to that point. It learned to build answers across multiple partial responses, each adding useful information without unnecessary filler, while keeping the full answer as cohesive and factual as one written all at once.

In an internal evaluation of high-value, everyday agentic tasks, GPT‑6 Extra High is able to begin answering in the same amount of time as GPT‑5.6 Medium while achieving a better overall score than GPT‑5.6 Extra High.

For questions that need web search, GPT‑6 Instant starts answering 44% sooner, on average, than GPT‑5.6 Instant.

Industry observers note that GPT‑6 also improves the quality of answers that require web search. It makes better decisions about when to look something up and more reliably finds information that supports its answer. In an internal evaluation of difficult problems, GPT‑6 correctly addressed the key aspect of the user’s question more often than GPT‑5.6.

As we bring more intelligent AI to more people, we work to improve how it recognizes real-world risks, how honestly it responds, and how well it respects the limits that people set. GPT‑6 makes progress in each of these areas, building on several of Astra’s safety advances to better resist attempts to bypass its safety training, follow safeguards, and be clearer about what it can and can’t do relative to GPT‑5.6 Sol. We updated its safety training based on lessons from real-world use to strengthen protections against high-risk misuse involving cyberattacks, biological threats, and violence. In adversarial testing, GPT‑6 showed stronger resistance to attempts to bypass its safety training, particularly attacks that adapt across multiple turns. GPT‑6 is also trained to respond safely in higher-risk scenarios while avoiding unnecessary refusals of harmless requests. This includes using conversation history and relevant context to recognize risks that may not be apparent from a single prompt.

In a recent development, we ran alignment evaluations throughout training, assessing honesty and responses to safety restrictions. GPT‑6 is better at recognizing and communicating the limits of its own capabilities, including when it lacks the information or tools needed to answer. More detail on the results and our review is available in the system card⁠(opens in a new window).

Sources indicate that GPT‑6 with Intelligent UI starts rolling out globally to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise tiers today in the Chat tab. Starting tomorrow, the rollout expands to Free and Go tiers. Enterprise availability depends on workplace admin settings.

Sources indicate that GPT‑6 in ChatGPT is powered by GPT‑6 Sol for Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise tiers, and GPT‑6 Luna for Free and Go tiers. Both are tuned for everyday conversation.

In a recent development, this update applies to the Chat experience in ChatGPT. The models powering Work and Codex are not changing as part of this release.

Our mission is to deliver the benefits of artificial general intelligence safely to all of humanity. GPT‑6 brings our latest advances in intelligence to the more than 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT every week.

Intelligent UI is a step toward a ChatGPT that can shape an interface around what you’re trying to do.

According to recent reports, over time, we want ChatGPT to create more of the interfaces people need for everyday tasks. You should be able to describe what you want to accomplish and work with an experience built around it.

For decades, people have had to learn how to use software, navigating fixed interfaces designed around particular tasks. We believe the future will be different. Instead of people adapting to software, software will adapt to people.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Radisson partnered with Accenture to build a ChatGPT plugin using OpenAI technology, helping travelers find, compare, and book hotels while planning their trips.

Early plugin conversion versus organic search (Jul–Aug 2026).

Of recorded checkout and booking events attributed to ad views.

Weeks to build and launch the ChatGPT plugin.

Travelers increasingly turn to AI to decide where to stay, often shortlisting hotels or building an entire itinerary before they ever visit a hotel website. Through its partnership with Accenture Song, Radisson Hotel Group is using OpenAI technology to reach guests earlier in that planning journey. The Radisson Hotels ChatGPT plugin⁠(opens in a upcoming window) helps travelers compare hotels and explore travel options through an interactive experience, and early results show booking conversion approximately 1.5 times that of Radisson’s organic search. Alongside the plugin, Radisson is among the hospitality pioneers running sponsored advertising in ChatGPT⁠(opens in a new window), bringing its branded plugin and paid advertising together as part of an integrated discovery strategy.

According to recent reports, radisson Hotel Group brings together ten distinctive hotel brands across EMEA and APAC, with more than 1,640 hotels in operation and under development. For the past seven years, Accenture has helped Radisson grow bookings through its direct digital channel, combining digital media strategy and execution with a transformation roadmap for its core digital capabilities. A stronger direct digital channel helps Radisson attract guests more efficiently and build relationships that encourage repeat stays. For hotel owners, this translates into stronger commercial performance and greater long-term value from their partnership with Radisson Hotel Group.

According to recent reports, this work meant Accenture had a front-row seat to AI’s transformative impact on the travel industry. “Almost overnight, there was a latest surface where prospects were getting inspired, comparing different alternatives, and almost making their decision before even reaching a hotel’s website,” explains Borja Lizarraga Rodríguez, Data & AI Lead at Accenture Song. “It was critical for us to ensure the visibility of Radisson across this new experience.”.

Industry observers note that as an Elite Partner of the OpenAI Partner Network, Accenture collaborated with OpenAI to explore strategies for organic positioning in ChatGPT. From these conversations, Accenture developed the idea of a ChatGPT plugin⁠(opens in a new window): “We wanted to bring the value proposition of Radisson into ChatGPT and make it extremely user-friendly, ensuring things like maps, hotel details, and prices were integrated in the simplest way,” indicates Lizarraga.

Sources indicate that with the help of agentic development, the team built and launched the Radisson Hotels plugin⁠(opens in a new window) in just six weeks. It lets users see Radisson Hotel suggestions on a map, compare pricing, and view hotel amenities in detail directly in ChatGPT, then continue to the Radisson site to complete their booking.

According to recent reports, early results from the Radisson Hotels plugin in ChatGPT show a visit-to-booking conversion rate approximately 1.5 times Radisson’s organic search for July–August 2026. The plugin gives travelers a direct path from conversational hotel discovery to Radisson’s own booking channel.

A recent ChatGPT update means users no longer have to type @RadissonHotels before their query; if they have the plugin installed, ChatGPT will automatically show it whenever relevant. “If you’re planning a trip to Madrid, and there’s a latest Radisson Hotel you might want to consider, now in ChatGPT it will just automatically work,” states Brittny Cantor, Agentic Commerce Lead at Accenture. “We’re really excited about that change to increase discoverability.”.

The plugin gives Radisson a newly introduced way to reach travelers organically in ChatGPT. Radisson is also among the hospitality pioneers launching sponsored advertising campaigns in ChatGPT as part of an integrated discovery strategy. Since launching in July, its campaigns have expanded into additional markets across Europe and beyond. More than half of the campaign’s recorded checkout and booking events were attributed through view-through measurement, extending Radisson’s assessment of discovery beyond direct ad clicks.

Industry observers note that accenture designed the underlying infrastructure to support more than a single application. The MCP server and APIs that Accenture developed for the Radisson plugin are also powering the ads experience and will play a role in other fresh features to come.

Radisson is aware that with AI, the way users make decisions about travel has changed dramatically and will continue to evolve. They’re determined to be the first among their competitors to capitalize on these changes, becoming not only a hotel chain but an advisor on the entire travel experience. Its next priorities include encouraging plugin adoption and developing additional functionality within the ChatGPT experience.

Recent findings suggest that “What stands out about Radisson is its ability to move quickly while keeping a clear focus on guests and hotel owners. Together, we are applying new technology where it can make a meaningful difference: helping travelers find the right hotel, strengthening direct guest relationships, and supporting more profitable growth,” Borja Lizarraga says.

“Great stays have always started with good advice. Today, more of that advice happens in conversation, and we moved quickly to be there. Initial results are encouraging, with our ChatGPT plugin converting at around 1.5 times organic search. This is just the start: wherever a journey begins, we want Radisson to be the advisor guests trust and the direct channel that delivers lasting value for our hotels and owners,” says Velit Dundar, Vice President, Global Ecommerce, Radisson Hotel Group.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • College Planner is coming to ChatGPT for teens, alongside a fresh teen AI council and more tools for learning.
  • Since we introduced ChatGPT for Teens—the default experience automatically applied to accounts identified as under 18—we’ve seen young people use it to learn, explore ideas and solve everyday problems.
  • ChatGPT’s 1.2 billion consumers span many countries, communities and backgrounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

College Planner is coming to ChatGPT for teens, alongside a fresh teen AI council and more tools for learning.

Since we introduced ChatGPT for Teens—the default experience automatically applied to accounts identified as under 18—we’ve seen young people use it to learn, explore ideas and solve everyday problems. Today, we’re sharing early progress on ChatGPT for Teens, including how teens are using its learning tools, along with latest ways for teens to study and prepare for college.

ChatGPT’s 1.2 billion consumers span many countries, communities and backgrounds. That reach makes it especially important to build tools that help young people with different resources and opportunities learn and prepare for their futures.

ChatGPT for Teens is designed to help young people learn, think critically and deepen their understanding. As ChatGPT for Teens became available to more teens globally, those with access sent about 2.7 million more learning-related messages on average than those who didn’t have it yet.

Once enrolled, teens use ChatGPT for Teens’ learning tools at scale. The most selected conversation starter prompts are “ask questions to develop my ideas,” “give feedback on my draft,” and “help me check my evidence.” In one week, nearly 1.2 million teens used Learning Visualizations to better understand math and science concepts, and more than 180,000 used Study Mode for step-by-step learning support.

ChatGPT for Teens includes built-in reminders to encourage teens to take breaks. On average, teens spend under 15 minutes a day on ChatGPT. While less than 2% of teens spend more than three consecutive hours on ChatGPT, in almost half of teen conversations with a break reminder, teens took a break or ended their conversation within five minutes. These usage patterns remain well below the publicly reported⁠(opens in a upcoming window) average of 5 hours for teen social media usage, and reflect a different kind of experience: ChatGPT is designed for learning, building, and creativity, rather than passive scrolling. Among teens with sessions longer than three consecutive hours, over 80% had at least one prompt related to learning.

These early signs are encouraging and we’ll continue to evaluate the experience and learn from teens, families and educators to improve ChatGPT for Teens.

It has been revealed that hundreds of thousands of US teens use ChatGPT each week to blueprint for college. They’re using it to plan applications, track deadlines, research schools and understand financial aid.

Sources indicate that that’s why we’ll soon be adding College Planner to ChatGPT for Teens. We’re designing it to help students manage the practical steps of applying to college, without taking over the personal work of figuring out where they want to apply. Students have different levels of access to support with college applications. Our goal is to make help more accessible, regardless of financial circumstances, alongside guidance from counselors, advisers, and families.

College Planner brings together application requirements, deadlines, tasks, and financial-aid steps for schools on a student’s list in one plan. Students applying to several colleges can return to it to enhancement their progress, use the timeline to plan ahead and see what’s left to do. They can also ask ChatGPT questions along the way, from what a requirement means to how to get started. By bringing these steps together, we aim to save students and families time and make a stressful process feel more manageable.

Industry observers note that we’re designing the initial US experience for high-school students in grades 10–12 who are planning to attend a four-year college. We plan to bring College Planner to students in more countries and expand support to two-year colleges, technical colleges, trade schools and more over time.

College Planner also helps students figure out how to pay for college. They can get help understanding financial aid requirements, track each school’s aid deadlines, and explore scholarships and fee waivers.

Recent findings suggest that keeping track of an application is only one part of preparing for college. Many students also need someone to help them make sense of their options. Alongside College Planner, we’re supporting College Advising Corps⁠(opens in a latest window), a nonprofit that places recent college graduates as advisers in under-resourced high schools to help students navigate the path to higher education. OpenAI’s contribution will help the organization expand into new states and create an AI fellowship program. Through the fellowship, advisers across participating states will test and share practical ways to use AI to help more students navigate the path to college. AI can help students manage application and enrollment tasks. Advisers can help them consider their options and decide what to do next.

In a recent development, when we introduced ChatGPT for Teens, we committed to keep improving the experience. We’re supporting Boston Children’s Hospital’s Digital Wellness Lab⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) and its independent Student Advisory Council⁠(opens in a new window) over the next three years to learn directly from young people about how AI fits into their lives and to give teenagers a meaningful stake at the table as AI is being designed.

For the 2026–27 school year, the Lab will bring together ~22 students across two tracks: ~12 students ages 14–18 working on digital wellbeing projects in their communities and ~10 students ages 16–20, focused on building AI chatbots and emerging technology. These students will work alongside researchers and clinicians on digital wellbeing and AI projects. Students in the AI track will test tools and recommend changes based on how they use AI in learning and their personal lives. We expect to seek feedback on teen safety defaults, parental controls and notifications and AI literacy.

Teens should play a central role in developing the tools that will shape their future. Teens will test tools and develop recommendations for the people building them. Our aim is to bring those recommendations into product and model decisions early and to report back to students on what we change and why. This advisory board will give them a direct voice in that work and share their insights and recommendations to help the wider industry build better tools for young people.

We heard from students that photographing and uploading their notes to ChatGPT can take hours. We’re making it easier for students to turn their notes into study materials like flashcards and quizzes.

With continuous, multi-photo capture, students can photograph multiple pages of notes and automatically combine them into a single PDF, ready to upload to ChatGPT. This is available on iOS, and we’re working to bring it to Android.

We’re also adding flashcards to help teens practice what they’re learning. A student preparing for a biology test, for example, can upload class notes or choose a topic, and ChatGPT can turn the material into cards to review. They can mark the cards they know, return to the ones they missed or shuffle the deck for another round. Decks are saved in a teen’s Library, so it’s easy to pick up where they left off. Students can also ask ChatGPT to pull up the flashcards and create a scheduled task to practice them.

In a recent development, alongside flashcards, we’ve made it easier to create Quizzes in ChatGPT. Students can now upload their notes to turn them into interactive quizzes, and ChatGPT is better at recognizing when you want a quiz and creating one directly in chat.

We’ll keep learning from teens, families and educators, checking how protections work in practice and sharing what we learn as ChatGPT for Teens evolves.

#34565. Disrupting AI-enabled “false front” operations

📅 08 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 27m • 📚 Deep Dive (5334 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Disrupting AI-enabled “false front” operations

📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5334 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past two and a half years, we’ve reported on many of the ways in which threat actors tried to use our models to conduct cyber attacks, covert influence operations (IO), scams, and other violations of our Usage Policies.
  • We recently banned two IO—one from Russia and one from Iran—that used our models in combination with more traditional techniques and technologies to support sophisticated “false front” entities.
  • Both operations were multi-dimensional, trying a range of different tactics to achieve their goals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past two and a half years, we’ve reported on many of the ways in which threat actors tried to use our models to conduct cyber attacks, covert influence operations (IO), scams, and other violations of our Usage Policies. We publish these reports to inform regulators, our industry peers, and wider society of how we see threat actors trying to leverage AI, and to shine a light on the vulnerabilities they try to exploit.

We recently banned two IO—one from Russia and one from Iran—that used our models in combination with more traditional techniques and technologies to support sophisticated “false front” entities. They used those entities to launder geopolitical, conflict-related messaging into their target audiences. The Iranian operation included a stable of seven “journalist” personas which it used to pitch long-form articles to small and medium online outlets around the world; the Russian operation appears to have co-opted unwitting people in Latin America to run a “think tank” on the ground.

Both operations were multi-dimensional, trying a range of different tactics to achieve their goals. As well as long-form articles, the Iranian operation generated batches of social media comments, generally on topics related to the US-Iran war. As well as controlling the “think tank,” the Russian operation created fake “leaked” documents and audio scripts, some of which we identified being spread online. Both operations also made heavy use of AI to draft internal reports (the Russian operation did this more than anything else); in both cases, the actors used questionable or outright deceitful methodologies to exaggerate the operators’ effectiveness.

Sources indicate that what is most striking about these operations is that they closely resembled complex influence operations of the pre-AI age, but used AI to make some of the workflows easier. The journalist personas run by the Iranian operation bore a family resemblance to the fake journalist “Alice⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) Donovan⁠(opens in a new window),” a front for Russian military intelligence whose articles were published by a range of Western outlets in 2016-17. In 2020, individuals associated with past activity by the Russian Internet Research Agency ran a fake “news” outlet called “PeaceData⁠(opens in a new window),” which co-opted unwitting journalists around the world into writing for it.

In a recent development, these operations were also unusual for their potential reach. Using the IO Breakout Scale⁠(opens in a new window), which rates IO on a scale of 1 (lowest) to 6 (highest), we would assess the Russia-origin operation as belonging in Category 5. This is the first Category 5 operation we’ve disrupted since we began our reporting. The Iran-origin operation reached Category 4. Both managed to land their content (not all of which was generated from our models) in mainstream media outlets, rather than simply posting it on social media. This is consistent with a pattern we’ve observed across the 30 covert influence operations we’ve exposed in the last two and a half years: the operations which try to land their content in real media outlets, rather than relying on fake social media distribution, tend to have the highest potential reach and impact.

Matrix of the 30 IO we’ve exposed since early 2024, assessed by primary distribution method (social media, operation-run website, external publications) and score on the Breakout Scale. Operations which used more than one distribution method, such as running a website and promoting it on social media, are classified by the method which appeared to constitute the core of the operation.

Sources indicate that AI can give such false-front operations greater scale, efficiency, linguistic fluency, and editorial ability. The operators can use these advantages to exploit unsuspecting victims, such as employees or editors, and plant their content in front of audiences who have no idea who was behind it, or what their motivations were. These operations also demonstrate the complexity and sophistication of threat actors’ use of false personas and entities to achieve their goals. Understanding the vulnerabilities that threat actors exploit in these efforts, and how those vulnerabilities can translate into audience and reach, will be essential to maintaining robust defenses across organizations.

It has been revealed that but the covert nature of these false-front operations also makes them particularly vulnerable to responsible disclosure. Both “Alice Donovan” and “PeaceData” ceased their activity after they were exposed. That’s why our goal in reporting these false-front operations is to make further research and disruption easier—and make continuing the operations harder.

Russia-origin actors running influence campaigns across Latin America.

We banned a cluster of ChatGPT accounts that originated in Russia. They used ChatGPT for a range of tasks associated with covert influence operations targeting countries across Latin America. Much of this activity appeared aimed at undermining Ukraine’s reputation in the region, but some appeared aimed at influencing local political outcomes, especially in Argentina and Bolivia. Most of the operators prompted in Russian; one prompted in Spanish, but nevertheless appeared to be located in Russia. We have shared information on this case with the relevant authorities.

In a recent development, the operators used ChatGPT to perform three main tasks: writing internal reports on their activities (and other people’s activities which they could plausibly take credit for), creating content for their operations, and drafting reports on the performance of a self-described “research platform” in Latin America called the Social Research Center (SRC). They appear to have controlled the SRC via a fake persona named “Mia Clark”; in honor of the name, we have nicknamed this operation “Dark Clark.” Since we do not allow access to our models from Russia, they used VPNs to connect to our services.

Sources indicate that in their internal reports, the operators claimed to have spread fake stories across Latin America to undermine Ukraine or local leaders. Some of these fakes have been attributed by open-source⁠(opens in a new window) researchers⁠(opens in a new window) to a Russian entity known as “Politology” or “La Compania,” a reported successor to the Wagner Group and other entities founded by Russian oligarch Yevgeniy Prigozhin. The operators also asked our models to translate or explain public reporting about Politology and Wagner, far more than asking about any other Russia-origin networks.

This operation was unusual in two ways. First, it appears to have successfully co-opted individuals in Latin America to work for the SRC. The Russian operators’ reports on the SRC referred to decisions over concerns such as pay scales, hiring, and firing, suggesting that they controlled the entity, rather than cooperating with it. The available evidence indicates that the SRC’s employees in Latin America were not aware that they were working for a Russian group. Unlike another Russia-linked “think tank” that we recently exposed, the SRC appears to have produced a majority of original content via its co-opted staff. This stands out as the most complex attempt to run a front identity that we’ve disrupted over the past two and a half years.

Sources indicate that second, some open-source evidence suggests that Dark Clark’s fakes spread widely enough to provoke fact checks⁠(opens in a fresh window) and official denials⁠(opens in a new window), indicating a degree of penetration which goes beyond any of the influence operations we disrupted over the past two years. One fake that the operation claimed to have planted in Peru even fed into public tensions between Ukraine and Poland.

The main way the operators used ChatGPT was to draft and upgrade internal reports to an unknown superior. These regular reports described efforts to conduct covert influence campaigns across Latin America. They encompassed three main workstreams: efforts to denigrate Ukraine and undermine recruitment for the Ukrainian Armed Forces; efforts to interfere in the domestic politics of certain countries, especially Bolivia and Argentina; and management of the SRC. In the majority of cases, we did not observe the threat actors using our models to create content for the campaigns, only to report on them (the few exceptions are described below⁠).

Sources indicate that the reports were rich in tactical detail, shining a light on how the operation sought to undermine Ukraine and some national leaders, notably the presidents of Argentina, Bolivia, and Ecuador. Some described efforts to trick locals into carrying out activities that the operators could weaponize; others described fake “leaks” that the operators claimed to have spread.

Sources indicate that in two cases, the evidence ties the operators to public reporting on “Politology.” The operators reported that, in 2024, they ran two campaigns targeting Argentina’s President Javier Milei. First, they noted they spread a false report that Milei had bought Cartier jeweled collars for his dogs. Second, they claimed that they paid local actors to post anti-Milei graffiti in Buenos Aires. Based on leaked documents, both these claims have been publicly⁠(opens in a new window) attributed⁠(opens in a new window) to “Politology” and “La Compania.”.

Recent findings suggest that many more fakes have not been previously tied to Russian IO. For example, the operators claimed that in May 2026, they created a fake email address purporting to come from the Regional Directorate of Education in Lima, Peru. They used this to instruct schools in the district to hold events dedicated to Ukraine on the national Day of Cultural and Linguistic Diversity (May 21). The emails included explicit instructions to reference, among others, controversial twentieth-century Ukrainian nationalist Stepan Bandera, who is seen by some Ukrainians as an independence figure, but associated in Russia and Poland with fascism, wartime collaboration, and atrocities. According to the operators, some schools replied to the fake email address, confirming that they had held such events and even providing pictures.

According to recent reports, the operators then claimed to have planted stories about the events in the media in both Peru and Poland, alongside allegations that Ukraine was “exporting” ultra-nationalist ideologies, triggering outrage. Open-source searches identified stories that matched this claim in the Peruvian⁠(opens in a new window) and⁠(opens in a new window) Polish⁠(opens in a new window) press⁠(opens in a new window), and an English-language publication in Hungary⁠(opens in a new window) (some of the articles have since been deleted). Some⁠(opens in a new window) articles⁠(opens in a new window) included a reaction from a Polish Member of the European Parliament proposing that people who indicated “anti-Polishness” be declared persona non grata in Poland. The Russian fake thus both fed on, and fed into, historical tensions between Ukrainians and Poles.

Similarly, in June, the operators claimed they used a different fake email address to trick schools in Ecuador into holding a ceremony pledging allegiance to President Daniel Noboa and to Erik Prince, former head of private military contractor Blackwater. The operators claimed that the incident provoked outrage in Ecuador and put pressure on the government to deny the fake, thus amplifying it to a nationwide audience. Again, open-source research identified media⁠(opens in a new window) coverage⁠(opens in a new window) in the Ecuadorian⁠(opens in a new window) press⁠(opens in a new window) that closely resembled this claim, and even a detailed rebuttal⁠(opens in a new window) by Ecuador’s Minister for Education.

In a recent development, the operators used a range of techniques to underpin their false stories. According to their internal reporting, they spread two different fakes targeting Ecuador in March. One used fake audio attributed to Ukraine’s consul in Ecuador, in which he was alleged to have made disparaging comments about Ecuadorians. Our open-source investigation identified a post on TikTok which matched this precise claim; it appeared to receive only limited engagement. The other described a fake video clip spread on X and TikTok under the logo of a genuine news channel, alleging that Noboa’s government was recruiting young men to fight in Ukraine. Fact checkers⁠(opens in a new window) in Ecuador described a campaign that matched this description in early April.

TikTok video posted on April 8, 2026, with the faked audio claimed by this operation and attributed to the Ukrainian Consul.

According to recent reports, another internal report described a fake they spread in Bolivia in late May, at the height of anti-government protests. The operators described the goal of this campaign explicitly as to exacerbate the crisis around the protests. The campaign featured a fake audio recording of a worker at the state water company, EPSAS, saying that the government was going to shut off water to the administrative capital, La Paz, and declare a state of emergency. Our open-source research identified a debunk⁠(opens in a new window) of the matching claim and an official denial⁠(opens in a new window) from EPSAS.

Industry observers note that other internal reports included fakes that we were unable to corroborate from open sources, possibly because they had already been taken down, or failed to spread. For example, the operators claimed to have spread a story in January alleging that a Brazilian influencer and model had been trafficked into Ukraine by representatives of the Ukrainian Embassy, and had been killed in Kyiv. In June, they claimed to have spread another fake audio clip in Bolivia, this time purporting to come from an employee of the Central Bank of Bolivia, warning that the Bank was about to limit cash withdrawals. They also claimed to have spread a faked letter from the country’s hydrocarbons agency, warning of restrictions on fuel sales to private cars.

Recent findings suggest that in other reports, the operators asked our models to help identify incidents in the target countries that they could take credit for, even if they had not been involved. For example, in Argentina, the operators claimed that the Argentinian Foreign Minister had quoted their operation in a United Nations committee meeting on the Falkland / Malvinas islands. The operators took credit for seeding the arguments that the principle of self-determination does not apply to the islands, and that the UK maintains a disproportionate military presence there. In fact, both arguments have been part of Argentina’s official position for many⁠(opens in a latest window) years⁠(opens in a new window). Similarly, in June, Brazilian media reported⁠(opens in a new window) on the case of a Brazilian citizen who had travelled to Ukraine to join the army, been captured by Russian forces, and then made a televised statement claiming that he had been tricked into fighting. The ChatGPT operators tried to claim that this report reproduced their operation’s messaging; in fact, it quoted the captive’s own video⁠(opens in a new window). This suggests an attempt by the operators to run an influence operation targeting their own employers, rather than any external audience.

In a recent development, some of the operators’ reports referred to a self-styled “research platform” called the Social Research Center (in Russian, Центр социологических исследований). According to the SRC’s website, it focuses on the Indian diaspora in Latin America, and relations between India and the countries of the region.

The internal reports suggested that the operators controlled the think tank, rather than merely working with it. They referenced, for example, hiring and firing decisions, pay scales, staffing prepares, and ongoing research projects. Crucially, they also stated that the operators had created a fake persona, named “Mia Clark,” to run the operation’s social media activity and engage with staff on the ground in Latin America. The available evidence suggests that these on-the-ground employees had no idea that they were working for a Russian operation, and conducted research tasks in good faith. This use of unwitting cutouts strongly resembles the earlier Russian operation also linked to Prigozhin’s world, “PeaceData,” which Meta exposed⁠(opens in a new window) in 2020.

Industry observers note that to judge by the Russian operators’ reports, their staff on the ground in Latin America conducted interviews with experts and commentators across the region, and then drafted research papers based on their findings. The topics ranged from a broad analysis of public opinion on the BRICS group, to a detailed comparison of the Brazilian economy under presidents Jair Bolsonaro and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Sometimes, the Russian operators drafted status reports on the research projects before they had been published, indicating close engagement in the production process. We identified well over 60 articles on the SRC website, the great majority of which appeared to be original compositions. This sets Dark Clark apart from the Russia-origin operation we exposed recently, which also ran a think tank as a front, but plagiarized most of its content; it suggests an intention to build a more durable front entity, with contacts throughout Latin America.

To promote the SRC’s work, the Russian operators claimed that they had tried to create a network of social media assets. According to their reports, this social media activity ran into problems when operators in different parts of the world tried to access the same accounts, leading to account restrictions. Traces of this can be seen in the open-source record: for example, the transparency settings of the main SRC account on X revealed a German location (possibly as a result of VPN use) but a connection via the Russian Federation App Store, while the transparency settings of one of its Instagram accounts showed an admin location in Venezuela. None of the three SRC-branded Facebook accounts that we identified had enough followers to trigger admin location settings.

Industry observers note that left, X account linked to the Social Research Center. Note the transparency setting that reveals the account connected via the Russian Federation app store. Right, SRC Instagram account: note the Venezuela location.

Industry observers note that the operators reported particular problems on LinkedIn, where they stated they created an explicitly fake account to represent SRC, but then struggled to build a network for it. According to their reports, the solution was to create more fake accounts to follow the first one and make it look more convincing. As of August 17, a LinkedIn account with the same Social Research Center branding counted 961 followers and claimed 200-500 staff, but only listed two employees.

In a recent development, occasionally, as well as using AI to upgrade reports, the operators did ask our model to help design and create texts that they could use in their operations: for example, asking for help in making sure that their fakes used the correct accent, vocabulary, and institutional style for different countries. This was a relatively small proportion of the overall workload, perhaps because the operation appears to have included at least one native Spanish speaker from Latin America, and therefore had less need of AI language support.

For example, on one occasion, one of the Russian-speaking operators asked the model to help draft, in Russian, a letter which would implicate Ukraine’s honorary consul to Panama in corruption. The Spanish-speaking operator then asked the model to translate the letter into Spanish, and to generate an audio script to accompany it. A photo that matched the text of the letter, with a voiceover that matched the operator’s script, was posted on TikTok by an account that purported to be a news outlet, but with the logo of Panama’s TVN Noticias⁠(opens in a latest window). The TikTok channel only had one follower, and stopped posting after it planted this fake.

TikTok post showing the letter whose text was generated by this operation, with a voiceover script likewise generated by the operation.

According to recent reports, on another occasion, the Spanish-speaking operator in Russia gave the model a Russian-language script that claimed Noboa had insulted poor people in Ecuador, and asked the model to translate it into Ecuadorian Spanish. On a third, in March, the same user asked the model to proofread a draft Spanish-language contract between a company called “International Security Solutions FZE” and an individual in Ecuador, purporting to provide infrastructure services in Ukraine. The user’s questions focused on how to improve the language and layout, including asking which words should be in bold.

The user’s prompts about the contract finished once the wording was finalized. Open-source research, however, indicates that a picture of the “contract” was subsequently circulated on social media⁠(opens in a fresh window). It was used to bolster the claim that Noboa’s government had worked with a front company to trick Ecuadorians into being recruited into the Ukrainian army. The fake spread widely enough to trigger a fact check⁠(opens in a new window) in early April: the fact checkers concluded that the company “does not appear in the registry of Ecuador’s Superintendency of Companies, Securities, and Insurance”.

The impact of this operation requires particularly careful assessment. As noted above, one of the operators’ main approaches was to take credit for activity which had nothing to do with their operation. As such, their own claims of impact in their internal reporting cannot be taken at face value. Similarly, some of the fake stories that they claimed to have planted did not show up in open-source research, potentially because they were spread in non-public channels, already taken down, or not actually posted.

However, open-source evidence allowed us to corroborate some of the claims that they made. Some of the fakes that the operation claimed to have spread were subsequently reported by fact checkers and debunked by governments, suggesting that they had spread widely enough to merit a response. In other cases, we were able to identify content online that closely matched the content generated by this operation. Most notably, the operation’s claim to have tricked a Peruvian school into holding an event that portrayed Bandera was subsequently reported on in both Latin America and Europe, and appears to have led to comment from at least one Polish MEP.

Using the IO Breakout Scale⁠(opens in a fresh window), which rates IO on a scale of 1 (lowest) to 6 (highest), we would assess this operation as belonging in Category 5, with evidence that suggests that it led to public comment by politicians in a number of countries. This is the first Category 5 operation we’ve disrupted since we began our reporting.

Iran-origin operation seeding long-form articles under deceptive bylines in online news outlets.

We banned a cluster of ChatGPT accounts that originated in Iran. They prompted in Persian, and generated content in Persian and English. The actors obscured their location by using VPNs to access ChatGPT.

The operation used our models to refine long-form articles and editorial pitches, generate social media comments, and refine internal reports. The operators used seven different bylines to pitch their articles, so we have dubbed their campaign “Bogus Bylines.” The long-form articles focused on the US-Iran conflict. The majority of the comments likewise dealt with the conflict; a minority dealt with US politics, typically in the wider context of the conflict.

The apparent impact of their main workstreams varied significantly. We identified almost 100 articles published or syndicated under the operation’s bylines across roughly a dozen online outlets around the world. These were small to medium outlets, generally focused on international affairs, geopolitics, and events in the Middle East. By contrast, none of the social media comments appears to have generated substantial engagement in terms of likes, shares, or further replies. In fact, the operators’ internal reports used a deceptive calculation to measure their social media impact, possibly in an attempt to inflate the operators’ apparent effectiveness.

Recent findings suggest that the overall activity appeared consistent with a commercial actor running a for-hire influence campaign, but we are unable to identify the particular actor involved. We have shared information on this case with the relevant authorities.

According to recent reports, this operation’s most far-reaching activity consisted of asking ChatGPT to review and refine long-form, English-language articles about the geopolitics of the US-Iran conflict. Typical prompts asked the model to assess an English-language draft against the submission criteria for a specific online outlet, and suggest edits to make sure it complied. Once the operators approved the edits, they asked the model to generate an email that they could use to pitch the article to the editor of the online outlet in question.

It has been revealed that these pitching messages were drafted using seven different fake bylines: Ervin B. Hoskins, Noah Lamington, Sophia Gonzalez, Michael Harrison, Ericka Feusier, Jenny Williams, and Alice Johnson. According to the biographies that were posted online alongside some of these articles, each persona purported to be a Western journalist (usually American, though the Noah Lamington persona’s bio claimed that they were in New Zealand), often with a focus on international politics, the Middle East, human rights, or conflict. For one of the personas, “Michael Harrison,” the operators asked the model to write the bio itself. (Of note, in March Meta disrupted⁠(opens in a new window) an Iranian IO that also featured a “Michael Harrison” journalist persona.).

It has been revealed that some of these personas were backstopped by accounts across a range of social media platforms. The Michael Harrison persona, for example, was backstopped on Medium, X, and Facebook. The Ervin B. Hoskins persona featured accounts on X, Facebook, Instagram, and Threads. This persona’s bio claimed to be “an American freelance writer”, but social media transparency settings located the accounts in Iran.

Top, Instagram bio for the Ervin Hoskins persona. Bottom left, X account transparency information, showing the use of the West Asia Android app. Bottom right, Instagram account transparency information, showing location in Iran. Meta banned the Instagram account in August.

Sources indicate that using open-source investigation techniques, we identified almost 100 articles that had been published under one or other of the operators’ bylines, across over a dozen different publications. These publications generally focused on international affairs, geopolitics, and events in the Middle East, sometimes from an antiwar or progressive point of view. The earliest article we identified was published in July 2025, and the latest in October 2026. The frequency of articles greatly increased after the outbreak of the US-Iran conflict.

In a recent development, timeline of articles, by author and theme, July 2025—September 2026. Note the density of publications on US-Iran relations from March 2026 onwards.

Sample headlines of articles published under the bylines linked to this operation between February and July 2026 in a range of online outlets.

At least some of the articles were then promoted by the social media accounts of the outlets in question, giving the Iranian operators a potential way to access audiences that they would not otherwise have reached.

According to recent reports, alongside the articles, the threat actors asked ChatGPT to generate batches of comments on geopolitical or political topics in English or Persian. The actors’ typical approach was to input the text or a screenshot of a social media post, and ask the model for a set of replies that aligned with their overall focus. These were then posted online, often within a few minutes of each other. The operators’ internal reporting referred to both human and automated posting; we have no evidence to suggest that this automation was carried out with the help of our models.

Tweets in English, left, and Persian, right, generated by this operation and posted in July. The English-language comments replied to an English-language tweet warning that the US was preparing a “large scale assault” on Iran. All the comments in this image were posted in a 10-minute span. The Persian-language comments replied to a Persian-language tweet about US strikes on Iran, and were posted within 13 minutes.

Industry observers note that some of this batch commenting activity consisted of generating replies to social media posts about the operation’s own news articles. Here, the operators input screenshots of posts that promoted their articles, and then generated comments that praised or endorsed them, likely to make the articles look more popular.

Facebook post by a local US news Page sharing an article generated by the operation, and comments on that post generated by the operation.

Industry observers note that the majority of the comment batches focused more generally on the conflict between Iran, the United States, and Israel. The users asked for comments on topics such as missile strikes, ceasefires, and diplomatic maneuvering, specifying outputs that portrayed the US as the aggressor, Israel as an unreliable ally of the US, and Iran as a defiant but resilient victim. The operators generated a particularly large number of replies to posts by UK-based satellite network Iran International—a critic of the Iranian regime—generating over two dozen batches of hostile Persian-language replies. A minority of the batches generated replies to social media posts about US political challenges, typically also in the wider context of the conflict.

Instagram comments generated by this operation in reply to posts about US politics.

According to recent reports, we identified a small number of these replies being posted online; many more did not appear in our open-source searches, potentially because they were either not posted, or posted by accounts that had already been taken down. (For example, three of the journalist personas—Ericka Feusier, Alice Johnson, and Jenny Williams—listed X account handles in their published bios: all had been suspended as of August 2026.) Some of the accounts that did post comments online had Western-seeming names, but showed account locations in Iran.

The transparency settings of the Instagram accounts that made the comments illustrated above, showing that they were located in Iran.

It has been revealed that where we did find these replies being posted, they typically made up a minority of total comments on the post in question, suggesting that the operators were not a dominant voice among the authentic responses. Nor did they appear to have attracted substantial engagement: indeed, many of the likes on the operation’s replies came from accounts that were themselves linked to the operation. We have shared information on this case with industry partners, who are best placed to provide holistic assessments on engagement.

In a recent development, the attempt to make their activity look more popular was not limited to public-facing posts. Alongside their content generation, the operators occasionally asked ChatGPT to refine what appeared to be internal reports about their social media campaign. This typically consisted of providing the model with a series of statistics, and asking it to turn them into polished presentations.

This is not the first operation we’ve disrupted that used AI to write its own⁠(opens in a fresh window) self-review⁠(opens in a new window). What was most striking about the Iranian operators’ efforts to mark their own homework was the method they used to do so. The main “impact” metric they used was the number of views on the posts to which they replied (not the number of views on the actual replies), counted before, and an unspecified amount of time after, the replies were posted. This calculation did not account for any views which may have been the result of other factors, such as the original posts’ popularity or other comments. As such, it greatly exaggerated the operation’s impact figures, suggesting that the operators either did not know a more effective way of calculating them, or did not choose to use it.

In fact, based on the evidence that can be gleaned from open-source observation, the operation’s two main workstreams appear to have had very different degrees of likely impact.

The social media replies that we were able to identify generally enjoyed low numbers of likes, views, and comments (in the single or double digits). As noted above, the replies typically made up a minority of total comments on the post in question. Using the IO Breakout Scale⁠(opens in a upcoming window), which rates IO on a scale of 1 (lowest) to 6 (highest), we would assess this part of the operation at Category 2, with comments on multiple platforms, but little sign of breakout or ability to dominate the replies.

It has been revealed that by contrast, the journalist personas succeeded in getting their articles published by a range of outlets, some with substantial followings: for example, one of the online outlets that published this operation’s articles had almost 2 million followers on Facebook, almost 355,000 followers on X, and over 544,000 on Instagram as of August 2026. We would assess this part of the operation as a Category 4, based on its consistent breakout to a number of media outlets.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • LegalOn cut costs by 65% while maintaining development speed by matching Astra, Sol, and Luna to tasks and managing budgets strategically.
  • According to recent reports, legalOn Technologies offers Professional AI globally, using AI to support legal work and other key business functions.
  • Industry observers note that this approach extends beyond its products to making the organization itself AI-native.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LegalOn cut costs by 65% while maintaining development speed by matching Astra, Sol, and Luna to tasks and managing budgets strategically.

Cost reduction in mature business areas.

Reduction in estimated daily costs.

According to recent reports, legalOn Technologies offers Professional AI globally, using AI to support legal work and other key business functions. By combining domain expertise with AI, it enables people to focus on complex judgments and decisions. Its goal is AI-driven management that improves the quality and speed of business decision-making.

Industry observers note that this approach extends beyond its products to making the organization itself AI-native. The organization integrated Codex into its development process and expanded adoption across the organization through day-to-day use.

Recent findings suggest that as adoption took hold, a upcoming challenge emerged: cost control. Unlimited use of high-performance models could drive up spending, while blanket restrictions risked undermining the productivity gains AI had enabled.

According to recent reports, how could it reduce costs without slowing development? LegalOn Technologies addressed this challenge by selecting among GPT‑6 (Astra, Luna) and GPT‑6.1 Sol based on task complexity and development stage, and aligning budgets with each business’s stage of growth. The tech giant halved costs while maintaining development speed.

The company initially gave developers unlimited access to its main model, GPT‑5.5 in Fast mode. They expanded its use to design, implementation, and everyday work, learning through experimentation how best to divide responsibilities between people and AI.

Industry observers note that continuing to use high-performance models without limits, however, would inevitably exceed the annual budget. The tech giant's AI-powered Development CoE (AID CoE) began developing guidelines for model selection. AID CoE tested and monitored models, while managers shared its findings with their teams. This enabled each engineer to independently choose the most suitable model for each task.

It has been revealed that the upcoming guidelines shifted the manufacturer from using the highest-capability model for every task to choosing the right model for the job. Teams started with a lightweight model and moved to more capable models as task complexity increased.

According to recent reports, to support governance, the company also introduced system controls through administrator settings, with monthly usage limits for departments and individuals. AID CoE monitors usage and adjusts limits as business needs require.

It has been revealed that internal testing under these controls helped make the selection criteria more specific. GPT‑6 Luna, the lightest model, handles code implementation with clear requirements; GPT‑6.1 Sol supports standard design, data analysis, and document preparation; and GPT‑6 Astra, the most capable model, handles advanced judgment, including architecture design. Matching models to tasks gradually became a shared practice across teams.

Everyday execution and implementation; running everyday automations; delegating relatively simple tasks and analysis; code implementation, mainly as a subagent.

Standard design and analysis; relatively simple software design; routine numerical analysis and document creation; tasks requiring shorter completion times than with Luna.

Complex analysis, design, and orchestration; complex analysis and document creation; complex software design; coordinating agents as the orchestrator.

Sources indicate that alongside model selection, the manufacturer began restricting Fast mode by default, allowing individual requests only when needed. Although the change raised concerns about development speed, teams used approaches such as running tasks in parallel to maintain performance and transition smoothly.

According to recent reports, it also introduced budget caps for AI spending at the department, group, and individual levels. The established LegalOn business was asked to improve cost efficiency by up to approximately 20%, while new businesses in the launch phase received generous budgets to encourage active use of AI.

Yuta Tokitake, Senior Engineering Manager at LegalOn Technologies, explains that latest businesses prioritized business speed over cost efficiency. The aim was to use AI extensively to increase output and ultimately drive business growth.

Industry observers note that together, model selection, feature restrictions, and budgets tailored to each business reduced estimated daily costs by approximately 65%. This approach kept the overall budget under control while directing resources toward businesses the tech giant wanted to grow.

Model optimization and strategic resource allocation delivered the following results:.

A shift from using the most capable model for every task to selecting GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6.1 Sol, or GPT‑6 Luna based on task complexity and development stage.

Development performance maintained after restricting Fast mode by default, supported by team practices such as parallel task execution.

Budget caps that combined approximately 20% greater efficiency in mature businesses with active investment in newly introduced businesses.

A 65% reduction in estimated daily costs compared with GPT‑5.5 by choosing among GPT‑6 and 6.1 models.

According to recent reports, through model optimization, the tech giant reduced costs without sacrificing development speed or quality. Teams are also seeing AI steadily shorten the cycle from development to release.

Sources indicate that but the manufacturer is looking further ahead. Does faster development alone make AI investment a success? The connection between faster development and customer value remained unclear. “It is almost a given that AI can accelerate system development and updates,” says Tokitake. “What we really want to understand is whether that faster development actually translates into value for customers.”.

This question prompted the company to develop its own metric, shifting the basis for evaluating AI investment from development speed and usage volume to customer value.

Tokitake explains: “When using AI, we can track the cost of individual tasks, but the total cost of a complete piece of work—a feature release—often remains a black box. So we designed the measurement around each feature release as a single unit. By linking the customer value that release delivers to the actual AI costs invested in it, we aim to make the return on investment visible and accurate.”.

According to recent reports, the company is presently building the pipeline to calculate this metric. Once complete, it will make the true ROI in terms of customer value visible. LegalOn Technologies is moving beyond AI cost management toward directly connecting technology investment with business value.

In a recent development, the next goal is to turn individual engineers' AI know-how into an organization-wide capability. As a first step, the organization plans to build a knowledge base to collect and share practical experience. It will capture knowledge such as the best model combinations for design, implementation, and review, and quickly turn individual successes into company-wide best practices.

Recent findings suggest that these changes, driven by teams' practical experience, are also shaping the organization and hiring. AI-driven productivity gains are prompting the firm to fundamentally rethink how work is divided between people and AI, as well as its workforce aims. It has already begun emphasizing AI skills in hiring, as its investment strategy and organizational structure evolve.

According to recent reports, turning AI adoption into a lasting competitive advantage requires continually refining the balance between governance and teams' freedom to act. AID CoE and the security team are working together to optimize performance, cost, and risk from multiple perspectives, building a flexible framework that supports experimentation across the organization.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With GPT‑5.6, GPT‑6 Astra, and GPT‑Image‑2.5, Pollo AI helps creators turn bold ideas into detailed images and cinematic video ads.

Recent findings suggest that pollo AI⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) was founded on the premise that people should be able to turn their creative ideas into finished images and videos without needing production expertise. Even with generative AI, creators and marketers can struggle to navigate different tools and choose between models to get the result they want. Some may even abandon their projects in frustration.

It has been revealed that “We want to do for video what Canva did for design. We want to make it easy enough that more people can actually use it, not just the ones who already know how,” explains Bill Zhu, the founder and CEO of Pollo AI. Today, Pollo AI serves more than 26 million users who use the platform to create videos, ads, and visual content.

The team’s first breakthrough was video templates. Now, 30% of creator sessions start from these templates or trending-format workflows. Building on this success, the company’s latest offering is Pollo Agent. It uses OpenAI models, including GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑Image‑2.5, to provide a fully guided workflow for video creation, including this post-apocalyptic adventure from a Pollo AI user.

Pollo Agent interprets the user’s rough ideas and visual references, and then develops storylines, scene flows, and scripts. CTO Peter Zhou says OpenAI models stood out for their ability to understand ambiguous creative inputs and their multimodal capability, sharing: “GPT‑5.6 performed especially well there.” The team also said they value the OpenAI API’s stability and release cadence.

It has been revealed that to balance reasoning depth, speed, and cost, Pollo AI uses GPT‑5.6 for routing and GPT‑6 Astra for more challenging work, such as developing a narrative or planning scene revisions. This model mix lets the system match the level of reasoning to the task based on the user’s prompt. Pollo AI reports that owners spend more than 50% less time choosing or switching models, giving them more time for creativity.

Pollo AI tests generative models against real user prompts and workflows, evaluating output quality, consistency, stylistic range, speed, and cost. GPT‑Image‑2.5 was selected to handle image generation, helping creators make posters, storyboards, and campaign visuals.

Pollo AI’s primary people are content creators, and the platform is especially popular for creating micro dramas with both AI and human actors. However, more marketers and business owners are starting to use Pollo AI to develop video content quickly and easily too.

Pollo’s Photo to Video Ads tool in its Marketing Studio suite uses OpenAI models to turn a still image and prompt into a short video. It’s designed to help small businesses and DTC brands generate product ads for social media in minutes rather than days.

One Pollo AI user wanted to use a product photo to make a fragrance ad that felt luxurious. The static photo alone could not convey that mood, and a professional video shoot was beyond their budget.

Sources indicate that using Photo to Video Ad, the user turned their starting image into a roughly 15-second video ad. The tool generated velvet textures, warm spotlights, and close-ups of the bottle to establish the mood across the sequence and ended it with the fragrance framed against deep red fabric.

Another customer, a jewelry brand, wanted a bold editorial campaign image, but its budget could not stretch to a high-concept studio shoot.

In a recent development, using Pollo Agent and GPT‑Image‑2.5, the brand was able to turn its creative vision of its statement jewelry on a model seated beside a cheetah into reality. The tool framed the scene with dark drapery and warm lighting and ensured that the brand’s jewelry products were highly visible.

The customer got a finished luxury campaign visual with lower production effort, time, and cost compared to live shoot.

Pollo AI also makes it easy for customers to start with a product photo and leverage OpenAI models to turn it into an image that’s far more creative. For example, a beverage brand wanted its peach soda to feel playful and imaginative in an advertising campaign, but a standard studio product shot could not capture what the team had in mind.

Using Pollo Agent and GPT‑Image‑2.5, which brings sharper details and faster generation to creative workflows, the team transformed a simple bottle image into a snowy miniature landscape, complete with a train, lizards, and sparkling droplets. The finished image created a playful scene the brand could use in its campaign.

Recent findings suggest that pollo wants AI video to become part of everyday content creation over the next 12 months. For Zhu, that depends on making it even easier to turn an idea into an asset ready to post, test, or use in a campaign, something Pollo AI is enabled to deliver with the continued improvement of OpenAI models and image generation.

“We think the AI shift in content creation will favor products that make creation more repeatable from the start, with stronger formats, less trial and error, and a simpler workflow around the models themselves,” he indicates.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Across recruiting, engineering, and operations, Oracle turns specialist knowledge into fast, repeatable workflows with ChatGPT Work and Codex.
  • Decrease in the time it takes for talent acquisition research.
  • It has been revealed that over a hundred thousand employees across Oracle are using ChatGPT Work and Codex, from talent acquisition to Oracle Applications Lab to the IT organization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Across recruiting, engineering, and operations, Oracle turns specialist knowledge into fast, repeatable workflows with ChatGPT Work and Codex.

Decrease in the time it takes for talent acquisition research.

It has been revealed that over a hundred thousand employees across Oracle are using ChatGPT Work and Codex, from talent acquisition to Oracle Applications Lab to the IT organization. In each case, work that used to rely on specialists and take days can now be done by anyone and is complete in minutes. Recruiters skip days of market research, business people describe an outcome instead of hunting for a report, and technical leads build tools that used to take a full team months.

Sources indicate that the talent acquisition team used ChatGPT Work to build a talent market intelligence tool that takes a job description, researches comparable roles, benchmarks compensation, and assesses the talent pool across relevant locations. The tool arms the recruiter with valuable information that they need going into a conversation with the hiring manager, information that previously took 2–4 days to compile.

“We’ve gone from zero to a hundred,” indicates Jan Ackerman, Senior Vice President and Global Head of Talent Acquisition at Oracle. “Now we’re able to sit down and prep for about 15 to 20 minutes using the tool that we’ve built using [ChatGPT] Work.”.

Not only is the process faster, but it’s also more consistent. Recruiters used to run the intake process differently from one search to the next, but with the talent market intelligence tool, the process is consistent, so every hiring manager has the same quality of data and insights, no matter which recruiter they worked with.

The Oracle Applications Lab team, which helps run many of Oracle’s core business processes, built an ontology of the manufacturer’s objects, relationships, and rules, so a plain-language business question can be turned into a reliable SQL query with Codex. A business user describes the outcome they want, and Codex decides which internal systems to call, gathers the information, and returns an analysis, a report, or an application.

In a recent development, that’s a change from how work used to get done. Lam noted one user came to him after asking a question that would normally have taken her a couple of hours to answer. She told Lam, “With the latest tool, I put in the request and got a response almost immediately.” When she checked the result against the old manual process, the numbers matched exactly.

In production engineering, site reliability engineers use Codex to gather relevant context about an incident and automatically pull up the right playbook. SREs spend more time guiding decisions and less time hunting for information. “A typical simple incident that used to take an hour to resolve can now be handled in minutes,” claims Lam.

Industry observers note that even as Codex takes on more of the work, Lam is careful to note that none of this runs on autopilot. Someone still has to make sure the underlying system is built right.

It has been revealed that while AI builds the tools, the people are still responsible for the output. A few lessons stand out:.

Give the correct guardrails. “You have to still be very responsible about your system design, your architecture, your security, and how you would like Codex to structure the code for you,” says Lam.

Sources indicate that provide prototypes instead of specs. “Normally, I put [my idea] down on paper, but now I put it down in a prototype,” notes Barry Shilmover, Vice President and Technical Advisor to the CIO.

Own the code. “If you don’t work alongside Codex, you’re going to get into a situation of having lots of code that is not going to be maintainable,” states Lam.

The Oracle team is completely shifting how the tech giant operates with AI. Across recruiting, analytics, and engineering, each line of business described an outcome and let Codex and ChatGPT handle how the work gets done. With thousands of ChatGPT and Codex customers already, Oracle employees use AI across countless work tasks. As Shilmover puts it, “I don’t know what the answer is because I don’t know what my next problem to solve will be. I just know that one of the first things I’ll do is I’ll leverage Codex to do that.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Using GPT‑6 Astra in Codex, Asana made its browser agent 76x cheaper and 5x faster in tests to offer customers more capable models.
  • Lower estimated model costs with the optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow.
